title: JFK (A): Who fired the shots?
question: Who fired the shots that struck President Kennedy and Governor Connally in Dealey Plaza on November 22, 1963?

hypotheses.text: Oswald alone fired all the shots, from the Book Depository's sixth floor
hypotheses.notes: Course Thesis 1 (lone gunman), as concluded by the Warren Commission.

hypotheses.text: Oswald fired, and at least one other gunman also fired (for example from the grassy knoll)
hypotheses.notes: The HSCA's 1979 conclusion (four shots, one from the knoll, which missed) and many conspiracy theses.

hypotheses.text: Oswald fired no shots; he was set up as the fall guy
hypotheses.notes: Oswald's own claim ("I'm just a patsy"); the planted-rifle, planted-bullet and impersonator theories (Syllabus, Appendix V).

evidence.text: A Mannlicher-Carcano rifle (C2766) was found hidden among boxes on the sixth floor; it had been mail-ordered under the alias "A. Hidell" to Oswald's post office box, and handwriting experts matched the order form to Oswald.
evidence.source: Warren Report ch. 4; Reitzes, Skeptic 18.3 (2013)
evidence.notes: Critics argue the rifle was planted; early reports called it a Mauser.

evidence.text: Three spent cartridge cases found by the sixth-floor southeast window were matched to that rifle to the exclusion of all other weapons.
evidence.source: Warren Report ch. 4; HSCA Report I.A

evidence.text: A nearly whole bullet (CE 399, found on a Parkland stretcher) and the two largest fragments from the limousine were matched to the rifle.
evidence.source: Warren Report ch. 4; HSCA Report I.A; Wikipedia, Single-bullet theory
evidence.notes: Chain of custody of CE 399 is disputed by critics.

evidence.text: Oswald's palm print was reported on the rifle's barrel, and prints on the trigger housing were later attributed to him.
evidence.source: Warren Report ch. 4; HSCA Report I.A
evidence.notes: The palm print was lifted by Dallas police and not seen by the FBI at first; critics question when it was taken.

evidence.text: Boxes were stacked into a sniper's perch at the southeast window, screened from the rest of the floor; Oswald's prints were on boxes there.
evidence.source: Warren Report ch. 4
evidence.notes: Oswald worked on that floor, which can explain prints on boxes.

evidence.text: Witness Howard Brennan saw a man fire a rifle from the sixth-floor southeast window; his later identification of Oswald was hesitant.
evidence.source: Warren Report ch. 3; Wikipedia, Howard Brennan

evidence.text: Oswald left the Book Depository within minutes of the shooting; about 45 minutes later Officer J.D. Tippit was shot, witnesses identified Oswald, shells at the scene matched the revolver Oswald carried when arrested in the Texas Theatre.
evidence.source: Warren Report ch. 4; Wikipedia, J. D. Tippit
evidence.notes: Bears on consciousness of guilt rather than directly on who fired in Dealey Plaza.

evidence.text: Oswald denied shooting anyone and called himself "just a patsy"; there are no recordings or transcripts of his roughly 12 hours of questioning.
evidence.source: Warren Report app. XI; Wikipedia, Lee Harvey Oswald
evidence.notes: Credibility here is that he said it, not that it is true.

evidence.text: The autopsy found the President was struck by two bullets from above and behind; review panels in 1968 (Clark), 1975 (Rockefeller) and 1978 (HSCA forensic pathology panel, 8 of 9, Wecht dissenting) agreed.
evidence.source: HSCA Report I.A; HSCA vol. 7 (medical panel); Wikipedia, Autopsy of John F. Kennedy
links: Wikipedia: Autopsy of John F. Kennedy

evidence.text: Parkland Hospital doctors and nurses described the throat wound as an entrance and a large wound at the back of the head, observations that suggest a shot from the front.
evidence.source: Warren Report ch. 3; Wikipedia, Autopsy of John F. Kennedy
evidence.notes: They were treating the President, not examining the wounds forensically; their accounts conflict with each other.
links: Wikipedia: Autopsy of John F. Kennedy

evidence.text: A 1993 JAMA study found trauma specialists misjudged gunshot wounds (entrance vs. exit, number of bullets) in 52% of fatal cases compared with forensic pathologists.
evidence.source: Reitzes, Skeptic 18.3 (2013)
evidence.notes: General reliability evidence; bears on how much weight a10 deserves.

evidence.text: The HSCA's photographic panel tested the autopsy photographs and X-rays and the "backyard" photographs for fakery and found none.
evidence.source: HSCA vol. 6 (photographic panel); HSCA vol. 7 (medical panel)
evidence.notes: Directly contrary to body- and photo-alteration claims (Thesis 7).

evidence.text: FBI agents Sibert and O'Neill, present at the Bethesda autopsy, wrote that there had been "surgery of the head area" before the autopsy began.
evidence.source: ARRB Final Report (1998); Wikipedia, Autopsy of John F. Kennedy
evidence.notes: The foundation of David Lifton's body-alteration thesis (Thesis 7). Others read it as recording a pathologist's first impression.
links: Wikipedia: Autopsy of John F. Kennedy

evidence.text: Lifton's thesis: the President's wounds were altered before the autopsy to hide shots from the front.
evidence.source: Wikipedia, Autopsy of John F. Kennedy; ARRB Final Report (1998); Lifton, Best Evidence
evidence.notes: An inference from a13 and the Parkland accounts, not independent evidence.
links: Wikipedia: Autopsy of John F. Kennedy

evidence.text: Of witnesses who gave an opinion, 81% heard three shots, 12% two, 5% four or more.
evidence.source: HSCA Report I.A; Reitzes, Skeptic 18.3 (2013)

evidence.text: Witnesses disagreed about where the shots came from, but very few said they came from more than one direction; Dealey Plaza's buildings produce strong echoes.
evidence.source: Warren Report ch. 3; Reitzes, Skeptic 18.3 (2013)

evidence.text: Some witnesses reported shots or smoke near the grassy knoll, and people and police ran toward the stockade fence after the shooting.
evidence.source: Warren Commission hearings and exhibits; Wikipedia, Dealey Plaza
evidence.notes: No one reported actually seeing a gunman there (Reitzes p. 10).

evidence.text: A search of the grassy knoll and stockade fence area found no weapon, shells or suspect.
evidence.source: Warren Report ch. 3

evidence.text: The Zapruder film shows the President's head moving back and to the left after the fatal shot.
evidence.source: Wikipedia, Zapruder film

evidence.text: Rockefeller Commission medical experts (1975) and the HSCA panel attributed the backward motion to a neuromuscular reaction, and noted a brief forward head movement between frames 312 and 313.
evidence.source: HSCA vol. 7 (medical panel); Wikipedia, Zapruder film
evidence.notes: Directly addresses how much weight a19 should carry.

evidence.text: HSCA acoustics consultants concluded from a police Dictabelt recording that four shots were fired, one from the grassy knoll ("95 percent" probability).
evidence.source: HSCA Report I.B; HSCA vol. 8 (acoustics; Ruby polygraph); Wikipedia, John F. Kennedy assassination Dictabelt recording; Ruby polygraph)
evidence.notes: The HSCA's "probable conspiracy" finding rested on this; three committee members dissented.
links: Wikipedia: John F. Kennedy assassination Dictabelt recording

evidence.text: The National Academy of Sciences' Ramsey Panel found the Dictabelt sounds were recorded about a minute after the shooting and were not gunshots; the FBI and Justice Department also disputed the HSCA analysis. A later reanalysis (Donald Thomas) disputes the NAS.
evidence.source: National Academies, Committee on Ballistic Acoustics (1982); Wikipedia, John F. Kennedy assassination Dictabelt recording
links: National Academies, Committee on Ballistic Acoustics (1982)
Wikipedia: John F. Kennedy assassination Dictabelt recording

evidence.text: The HSCA's photogrammetry (20-expert panel) and trajectory analysis (NASA engineer Thomas Canning) supported the single-bullet explanation; later 3D reconstructions agreed.
evidence.source: HSCA Report I.A; HSCA vol. 6 (photographic panel)
evidence.notes: The single-bullet explanation is what makes one gunman's timing possible.

evidence.text: Governor and Mrs. Connally testified in 1964 and again in 1978 that he was hit by a separate bullet from the one that first hit the President.
evidence.source: Warren Report ch. 3; HSCA Report I.A
evidence.notes: Honest eyewitness belief; whether a wounded man can time his own wound is the question.

evidence.text: The Zapruder film limits all the shots to a few seconds; the Warren Commission and HSCA judged three shots from the bolt-action rifle feasible in that time, which critics dispute.
evidence.source: Warren Report ch. 3; HSCA Report I.A; Wikipedia, Zapruder film

evidence.text: Oswald qualified as a "sharpshooter" (1956) and later "marksman" (1959) in the Marine Corps.
evidence.source: Warren Report ch. 4

evidence.text: Marina Oswald testified that she took the "backyard" photographs of Oswald holding the rifle and revolver.
evidence.source: Warren Report ch. 4; HSCA vol. 6 (photographic panel)
evidence.notes: Question 6 asks whether these were faked; see a12.

evidence.text: Marina Oswald testified, supported by documents, that Oswald fired at Gen. Edwin Walker in April 1963.
evidence.source: Warren Report ch. 4
evidence.notes: Shows willingness and ability to attempt a rifle shooting.

evidence.text: Dallas police paraffin tests were positive on Oswald's hands and negative on his cheek; the test is unreliable and the Warren Commission did not rely on it.
evidence.source: Warren Report ch. 4; Wikipedia, Gunshot residue

evidence.text: James Tague was slightly wounded by a fragment or ricochet near the triple underpass, showing that at least one shot missed or broke up.
evidence.source: Warren Report ch. 3; Wikipedia, James Tague

evidence.text: The "three tramps" taken from a boxcar near the knoll were identified from Dallas police files released in 1989 as transients Doyle, Abrams and Gedney.
evidence.source: HSCA Report I.A; Wikipedia, Three tramps
evidence.notes: Rules out the identifications as Hunt, Sturgis or Harrelson (Question 8).

evidence.text: Figures "found" in enlargements of the Moorman photo ("Badge Man" and others) were judged photographic artifacts; Lifton himself concluded enlargements had very limited value.
evidence.source: HSCA vol. 6 (photographic panel); Wikipedia, Badge Man

evidence.text: The "Umbrella Man" was identified as Louie Steven Witt, who testified to the HSCA that the umbrella was a political protest.
evidence.source: HSCA Report I.A; Wikipedia, Umbrella man (JFK assassination)

evidence.text: Critics document chain-of-custody gaps and handling problems in key exhibits (the stretcher bullet, the palm print, the autopsy materials).
evidence.source: ARRB Final Report (1998); Wikipedia, Single-bullet theory
evidence.notes: Bears on whether a01–a04 could have been planted.

evidence.text: Oswald's coworker Buell Wesley Frazier and his sister Linnie Mae Randle saw Oswald carry a long paper package to work that morning; Oswald said it held curtain rods. No curtain rods were found at the Depository, and his rooming house room already had curtains.
evidence.source: Warren Report ch. 4; Warren Commission hearings and exhibits
evidence.notes: Frazier and Randle both judged the package shorter than the disassembled rifle.

evidence.text: A long homemade paper bag with Oswald's fingerprint and palm print was reported found near the sixth-floor window. It does not appear in the earliest crime-scene photographs, and a replica made on December 1 from the shipping room's paper had different characteristics.
evidence.source: Warren Report ch. 4
evidence.notes: Critics question when the bag was found and whether it held the rifle.

evidence.text: An undeliverable, unstamped package addressed to "Lee Oswald" at a nonexistent Dallas address, containing a similar open-ended paper bag, was found in the Irving post office in December; no one remembered handling it.
evidence.source: Warren Commission hearings and exhibits; Mary Ferrell Foundation archive
evidence.notes: Sylvia Meagher argued only someone involved could have known in advance that a paper bag would become evidence.

evidence.text: Oswald was the only Depository employee known to have left the building after the shooting without permission and not returned.
evidence.source: Warren Report ch. 4

evidence.text: Officer Marrion Baker and manager Roy Truly met Oswald in the second-floor lunchroom about 90 seconds after the shots; he was calm and not out of breath. The Warren Commission's reconstruction found he could have got there from the sixth floor in time.
evidence.source: Warren Report ch. 4
evidence.notes: Critics say the timing is very tight and that Oswald's calm demeanor argues against his having just fired.

evidence.text: Carolyn Arnold, a Depository secretary, told the FBI on November 26 she glimpsed Oswald on the first floor between about 12:15 and 12:25. A later FBI statement has her saying otherwise, and she was not called as a witness.
evidence.source: Warren Commission hearings and exhibits; Mary Ferrell Foundation archive
evidence.notes: If accurate, it leaves little time to reach the sixth floor before 12:30.

evidence.text: Depository employees Bonnie Ray Williams, Harold Norman and James Jarman watched from the fifth-floor window directly below; Norman said he heard the rifle bolt and cartridges hitting the floor above.
evidence.source: Warren Report ch. 4

evidence.text: A Secret Service report quotes Harold Norman saying the shots came from directly above and dust fell from the ceiling; before the Warren Commission he denied saying so.
evidence.source: Warren Commission hearings and exhibits; Mary Ferrell Foundation archive

evidence.text: Williams ate lunch on the sixth floor until about 12:15 and saw no one there; chicken bones and a lunch bag were found near the window.
evidence.source: Warren Report ch. 4
evidence.notes: Hoover told RFK that Oswald had been eating chicken, which Williams's account refutes.

evidence.text: Three FBI master marksmen fired Oswald's rifle at stationary targets 45 feet away on November 27; none got three shots off within 5.6 seconds and all shot high and right. Later Warren Commission tests at longer range had riflemen meet the time.
evidence.source: Warren Report app. X; Wikipedia, Carcano
evidence.notes: The time required depends on whether the first shot missed and on the Zapruder timing.

evidence.text: The rifle's telescopic sight was found to be misaligned when tested and had to be shimmed before the FBI could fire accurately.
evidence.source: Warren Report app. X
evidence.notes: Whether it was knocked out of alignment after the shooting is unknown.

evidence.text: Dallas police and deputies Seymour Weitzman, Eugene Boone and Roger Craig first described the rifle found on the sixth floor as a 7.65 Mauser; DA Henry Wade repeated this on secondhand information.
evidence.source: Warren Report ch. 4; Wikipedia, Carcano
evidence.notes: Weitzman later said he was mistaken; the found rifle bears Carcano markings.

evidence.text: An FBI envelope labeled "7.65 shell found in Dealey Plaza on 12/02/1963," marked of no value and destroyed, surfaced only in 1995.
evidence.source: ARRB Final Report (1998); Mary Ferrell Foundation archive

evidence.text: Lt. J.C. Day said he lifted Oswald's palm print from the rifle barrel on November 22, but did not mention it then, and the FBI did not receive the lift until November 29; the FBI found no trace of the print or lift on the rifle.
evidence.source: Warren Report ch. 4; HSCA Report I.A
evidence.notes: The HSCA accepted the print as genuine.

evidence.text: FBI agent Richard Harrison said he drove another agent with the rifle to the funeral home holding Oswald's body, reportedly to take his palm print "for comparison purposes."
evidence.source: Mary Ferrell Foundation archive; Wikipedia, Lee Harvey Oswald
evidence.notes: Funeral director Paul Groody said the FBI fingerprinted the body.

evidence.text: Oswald's clipboard, with three unfilled orders dated November 22, was found hidden near the rifle location on December 2, after searches had missed it.
evidence.source: Warren Report ch. 4

evidence.text: Deputy Roger Craig said he saw a man resembling Oswald run down the slope and get into a light Rambler station wagon about 15 minutes after the shots, and identified Oswald in Fritz's office; others, including Fritz, disputed his account.
evidence.source: Warren Commission hearings and exhibits; Wikipedia, Roger D. Craig
evidence.notes: If true, Oswald left by car with someone else, not by bus and taxi.

evidence.text: Bus driver Cecil McWatters identified the transfer found on Oswald as one he issued on his route that afternoon, and passenger Mary Bledsoe said Oswald boarded the bus.
evidence.source: Warren Report ch. 4

evidence.text: Taxi driver William Whaley said he drove Oswald to Oak Cliff after the bus stalled in traffic.
evidence.source: Warren Report ch. 4

evidence.text: Housekeeper Earlene Roberts saw Oswald come home about 1 PM, grab a jacket and leave; she said a police car stopped and honked outside while he was there.
evidence.source: Warren Report ch. 4
evidence.notes: The honking police car has never been explained.

evidence.text: Several witnesses, including Helen Markham, the Davis sisters-in-law, William Scoggins and Ted Callaway, identified Oswald as Tippit's killer or the man fleeing with a pistol.
evidence.source: Warren Report ch. 4; Wikipedia, J. D. Tippit
evidence.notes: Markham's first lineup identification was shaky.

evidence.text: Cartridge cases found at the Tippit scene were matched to Oswald's revolver to the exclusion of all others; the bullets in Tippit's body could not be conclusively matched.
evidence.source: Warren Report ch. 4; HSCA Report I.A
evidence.notes: Dallas police gave the cases to the FBI only on November 26, and critics say initial reports described automatic-pistol shells.

evidence.text: At the Texas Theatre Oswald punched an arresting officer and drew his revolver.
evidence.source: Warren Report ch. 4

evidence.text: Oswald was arrested carrying a card in the name "A.J. Hidell," the alias used to order the rifle and pistol; a forged vaccination certificate signed "Dr. A.J. Hidell" was in his handwriting.
evidence.source: Warren Report ch. 4
evidence.notes: The "Hidell" card was not publicized at first, unlike the alias "O.H. Lee."

evidence.text: Oswald told police he did not own a rifle, denied having been on the sixth floor, and denied the backyard photographs were of him.
evidence.source: Warren Report app. XI

evidence.text: Oswald lied about several facts during questioning, such as the curtain rods and ownership of the rifle, according to the officers present; no recordings or verbatim notes exist.
evidence.source: Warren Report app. XI

evidence.text: Fibers on the rifle butt plate were consistent with the shirt Oswald wore when arrested.
evidence.source: Warren Report ch. 4
evidence.notes: Consistent with, not uniquely matched to.

evidence.text: The HSCA photographic panel examined the backyard photographs and the camera and found no signs of fakery; the camera was linked to Oswald.
evidence.source: HSCA vol. 6 (photographic panel)

evidence.text: Commercial photographer Robert Hester and his wife said an FBI agent had a color transparency of a backyard photo on the night of November 22, and that one print showed no figure, before the photos were officially found.
evidence.source: Mary Ferrell Foundation archive

evidence.text: The first search of the Paine garage on November 22 found no backyard photographs; police reported finding two prints and a negative the next day.
evidence.source: Warren Report ch. 4; Mary Ferrell Foundation archive

evidence.text: Marina Oswald told the Secret Service on December 1 she had never seen a scoped rifle before the assassination or her husband with a pistol, which conflicts with her later account of taking the backyard photographs.
evidence.source: Warren Commission hearings and exhibits; Wikipedia, Marina Oswald Porter

evidence.text: Many Dealey Plaza witnesses, including people on the knoll and railroad workers such as Sam Holland and Lee Bowers, reported shots, a puff of smoke or activity behind the stockade fence.
evidence.source: Warren Commission hearings and exhibits; Wikipedia, Dealey Plaza

evidence.text: Witnesses Jean Hill and others described a shooter or flash on the knoll; Hill said FBI chief Shanklin later pressed her to alter her account.
evidence.source: Warren Commission hearings and exhibits; Wikipedia, Jean Hill

evidence.text: Parkland doctors McClelland, Jenkins and Giesecke, and others, described a left-temple wound or damage to the left of the head in early statements.
evidence.source: Warren Commission hearings and exhibits; Wikipedia, Autopsy of John F. Kennedy
evidence.notes: The autopsy records no left-side wound.
links: Wikipedia: Autopsy of John F. Kennedy

evidence.text: Most Parkland staff described a large wound at the right rear of the head, consistent with an exit for a shot from the front; autopsy witnesses' drawings also placed the defect at the rear.
evidence.source: ARRB Final Report (1998); HSCA vol. 7 (medical panel)
evidence.notes: The autopsy photographs show the scalp at the back intact.

evidence.text: Gawler's morticians described an orange-sized hole only at the back of the head, plus a small wound at the right temple filled with wax.
evidence.source: ARRB Final Report (1998); Wikipedia, Autopsy of John F. Kennedy
links: Wikipedia: Autopsy of John F. Kennedy

evidence.text: Dr. Malcolm Perry told the press on November 22 that the throat wound looked like an entrance wound; he later said he could not be sure.
evidence.source: Warren Report ch. 3; Wikipedia, Malcolm Perry
evidence.notes: Agent Elmer Moore later said he worked on the Dallas doctors' testimony.

evidence.text: Dr. Robert Livingston said he phoned Dr. Humes before the autopsy to stress that the throat wound appeared to be an entrance, and that Humes broke off saying the FBI would not let him talk.
evidence.source: ARRB Final Report (1998); Mary Ferrell Foundation archive

evidence.text: The autopsy did not dissect the throat wound or trace the bullet track; Dr. Finck testified they were told not to, and corpsman Paul O'Connor said Adm. Galloway stopped the doctors.
evidence.source: Warren Commission hearings and exhibits; HSCA vol. 7 (medical panel)

evidence.text: Dr. Humes burned his original autopsy notes and the first draft of his report.
evidence.source: Warren Commission hearings and exhibits; Wikipedia, Autopsy of John F. Kennedy
evidence.notes: Humes said he did so because they were bloodstained.
links: Wikipedia: Autopsy of John F. Kennedy

evidence.text: Photographs of the chest interior and of beveling on the skull, which several witnesses say were taken, are not in the National Archives inventory; Kennedy's brain and tissue slides were found missing in 1966.
evidence.source: ARRB Final Report (1998)

evidence.text: Navy photo lab technician Saundra Spencer told the Review Board the autopsy prints she developed on November 23 differ from those in the official record.
evidence.source: ARRB Final Report (1998)

evidence.text: FBI agents Sibert and O'Neill reported that the back wound was shallow, with no exit, and the FBI's December 9 summary report said the same; the Warren Report later had that bullet exit the throat.
evidence.source: ARRB Final Report (1998); HSCA vol. 7 (medical panel)

evidence.text: A receipt signed by Secret Service official Robert Bouck acknowledges "a missile removed during the examination of the body," though officially no bullet was recovered at autopsy.
evidence.source: ARRB Final Report (1998); Mary Ferrell Foundation archive
evidence.notes: Some argue the receipt refers to fragments.

evidence.text: Admiral David Osborne and autopsy technicians said a bullet fell from the body or wrappings at Bethesda; the official chain of custody never takes CE 399 to Bethesda.
evidence.source: HSCA vol. 7 (medical panel); Mary Ferrell Foundation archive

evidence.text: Parkland employees who handled CE 399, Darrell Tomlinson and O.P. Wright, could not identify it, and the stretcher it was found on may not have been Connally's.
evidence.source: Warren Commission hearings and exhibits; Wikipedia, Single-bullet theory

evidence.text: Army wound-ballistics consultant Dr. Joseph Dolce said tests showed shooting a wrist badly deforms the bullet, so CE 399 could not have caused all of Connally's wounds; he was not called by the Warren Commission.
evidence.source: Mary Ferrell Foundation archive; Wikipedia, Single-bullet theory

evidence.text: Neutron activation analysis for the HSCA (Guinn) grouped the fragments into two bullets consistent with Oswald's ammunition; later studies questioned the method's statistics.
evidence.source: HSCA Report I.A; Wikipedia, Single-bullet theory

evidence.text: Agent Charles Taylor's report, reporter Richard Dudman and officers H.R. Freeman and Stavis Ellis described a hole in the limousine windshield; the FBI found only cracks and the windshield in evidence has no hole.
evidence.source: Warren Commission hearings and exhibits; Mary Ferrell Foundation archive
evidence.notes: A Ford employee later said a holed windshield was used as a template for a replacement.

evidence.text: The limousine was cleaned, stripped and rebuilt within weeks, before most forensic examination could be repeated.
evidence.source: Wikipedia, SS-100-X

evidence.text: Agent Clint Hill and Secret Service agents and police on the follow-up car described the final shot's impact and debris; motorcycle officers Hargis and Martin, to the left rear, were splattered.
evidence.source: Warren Report ch. 2; Warren Commission hearings and exhibits
evidence.notes: Critics read the spray to the left rear as evidence of a shot from the front right.

evidence.text: A fragment of skull found in Dealey Plaza the next day (the Harper fragment) was identified by pathologists as occipital (rear) bone in some analyses and parietal in others.
evidence.source: HSCA vol. 7 (medical panel)

evidence.text: Dan Rather, describing the Zapruder film on November 23, said the President's head went forward violently; the extant film shows a back-and-left motion after a brief forward movement.
evidence.source: Wikipedia, Zapruder film
evidence.notes: Rather later said he misdescribed it.

evidence.text: Orville Nix's film, measured against the Zapruder film, shows the limousine moving more slowly, which some researchers cite as evidence of film alteration.
evidence.source: Wikipedia, Zapruder film

evidence.text: Life described the film as showing Kennedy turning toward the sniper's nest before being hit in the throat, which the film does not show.
evidence.source: Wikipedia, Zapruder film

evidence.text: A WFAA cameraman was handed a 30.06 cartridge a mailman said he found in bushes near the Depository; no bushes lie below the window and a 30.06 cannot be fired in a Carcano.
evidence.source: Mary Ferrell Foundation archive

evidence.text: A loaded .38 Smith & Wesson revolver in a paper sack was turned in near Ross and Lamar the next morning; there is no record of what the FBI concluded.
evidence.source: Mary Ferrell Foundation archive

evidence.text: Dallas Morning News staff photographed a pool of blood found in the plaza; men identifying themselves as FBI agents took the negatives and told them it never happened.
evidence.source: Mary Ferrell Foundation archive

evidence.text: Witness Howard Brennan, who was not wearing his glasses, failed to identify Oswald at a lineup, said in December he was sure, then in January said he could not be positive.
evidence.source: Warren Report ch. 3; Wikipedia, Howard Brennan

evidence.text: Witness Ronald Fischer and others saw a man in a sixth-floor window whose description did not entirely match Oswald; Arnold Rowland saw a man with a rifle at the west end of the floor and an older man at the east window.
evidence.source: Warren Commission hearings and exhibits; Warren Report ch. 3

evidence.text: Photographs taken right after the shots show figures in the sixth-floor window area and boxes moved; HSCA analysts found movement in the window in the Hughes and Bronson films.
evidence.source: HSCA vol. 6 (photographic panel)

evidence.text: Seventeen cartridge clips or extra ammunition were never found in Oswald's possessions; only four rounds (three spent, one live) are accounted for.
evidence.source: Warren Report ch. 4

evidence.text: No record shows Oswald practiced with the rifle in the months before the assassination, though witnesses later said they saw a man resembling him at a rifle range.
evidence.source: Warren Report ch. 7

evidence.text: Oswald's Marine scorebooks show a declining score, and fellow Marine Nelson Delgado described him as a poor shot.
evidence.source: Warren Report ch. 4; Warren Commission hearings and exhibits
evidence.notes: Others note that "marksman" was still a passing qualification.

evidence.text: Mike Robinson, a teenager, said he overheard men at police headquarters complain that "Lee" was supposed to be killed, not a policeman; he came forward in 1993.
evidence.source: Mary Ferrell Foundation archive

evidence.text: Sgt. Robert Vinson claimed a military plane picked up two men, one resembling Oswald, by the Trinity River that afternoon; he kept silent until the 1990s.
evidence.source: Mary Ferrell Foundation archive

evidence.text: The HSCA concluded on the acoustic evidence that a second gunman probably fired from the knoll but missed; it found no other evidence of who that was.
evidence.source: HSCA Report I.B; HSCA vol. 8 (acoustics; Ruby polygraph); Ruby polygraph)

evidence.text: Both the Warren Commission and the HSCA found Oswald fired the shots that killed Kennedy and wounded Connally; the HSCA's medical panel found both hits came from behind.
evidence.source: Warren Report; HSCA Report I.A

evidence.text: Officials pressed early for a lone-gunman conclusion: Katzenbach's November 25 memo said the public must be satisfied Oswald was the assassin, and Hoover leaked that finding before the FBI report was delivered.
evidence.source: Wikipedia, Nicholas Katzenbach; Church Committee Book V (1976)
evidence.notes: Speaks to how the evidence was handled, not directly to who fired.

evidence.text: Hoover told Johnson on November 23 the case against Oswald was "not very, very strong," placing the shots on the fifth floor; his November 29 account to Johnson contained several errors.
evidence.source: Miller Center, Johnson telephone recordings; Church Committee Book V (1976)

evidence.text: The Dallas police radio Dictabelts were reportedly borrowed by federal agents soon after the assassination, raising chain-of-custody questions for the acoustic evidence.
evidence.source: National Academies, Committee on Ballistic Acoustics (1982); HSCA vol. 8 (acoustics; Ruby polygraph); Ruby polygraph)
links: National Academies, Committee on Ballistic Acoustics (1982)

evidence.text: Oswald asked repeatedly for a lawyer and never received one; he was interrogated about twelve hours with no recording.
evidence.source: Warren Report app. XI; Warren Report ch. 5
